name: Enzyme peel (papaya/pumpkin)

lead: An enzyme peel uses fruit enzymes, most often papain from papaya or enzymes from pumpkin or pineapple, to loosen dead surface cells for smoother, brighter skin and softer texture. It is marketed as a gentler alternative to acid peels.

Papain is a cysteine protease that breaks peptide bonds in protein. A 2022 laboratory study of eleven commercial products advertised as enzymatic found only two showed sufficient protease activity against casein, a generic protein substrate. No human clinical trial of enzyme peels was identified.

paras: Users apply the mask to clean skin, leave it for the time on the label and rinse it off, typically once a week, as a milder step than acids or scrubs.
Papain has been linked to allergic hypersensitivity reactions, and people with latex allergy may be at higher risk of reacting to papaya. Product enzyme activity varies.

angle.text: Papaya and pumpkin enzyme peels loosen dead surface cells without acids, so skin feels smoother and looks brighter. A 2022 lab study found most tested products had low enzyme activity, and human skin trials were not found.

lead: An enzyme peel is a rinse-off exfoliating mask built around fruit-derived protein-digesting enzymes, most often papain from papaya, bromelain from pineapple, or enzymes from pumpkin. People use it to loosen and lift the dead cells sitting on the skin's surface, aiming for a smoother, brighter, more even-looking complexion with less stinging and redness than an acid peel can bring.

Papain is a cysteine protease obtained from papaya latex that breaks peptide bonds in proteins [1]. Bromelain is a similar mixture of protein-digesting enzymes from pineapple, and extracted bromelain is used in cosmetics manufacturing among other industries [2]. In an enzyme peel the idea is that these proteases act on the protein bonds holding surface cells together, so the dead layer comes away with a short-contact mask. Papain was used in South America before European contact to tenderize meat, and its commercial uses now span food, leather, textile, detergent, pharmaceutical and cosmetic industries [1].

Enzyme peels sit at the gentle end of the exfoliation range. Chemical peel references describe alpha hydroxy acid and beta hydroxy acid peels as the mildest acid categories, with deeper retinoic acid, trichloroacetic acid and phenol peels at the other end [3]. Research on the cosmetic products themselves is limited to a 2022 laboratory study of eleven commercial peels advertised as enzymatic, which measured their protease activity against casein, a generic protein substrate, and compared them with fresh pineapple and papaya [4].
infobox: FDA warned against unapproved topical papain drugs, 2008 [1]

paras: Enzyme peels are applied as masks and rinsed off after a short contact time. Chemical peel references describe alpha hydroxy acid and beta hydroxy acid peels as the mildest acid peel categories, with stinging, redness and dryness as expected light effects [3]. Enzyme peels are marketed as an option that exfoliates through protein digestion instead of acidity, though enzyme peels are not themselves covered in that reference.

Pumpkin enzyme peels are usually sold alongside fruit acids and are popular in at-home facial care; papaya and pineapple masks draw on the long commercial use of papain and bromelain in cosmetics [1][2].

sections.h: Where enzyme peels fit among peels
paras: Chemical peeling as a medical practice goes back to the second half of the 19th century, when the Austrian dermatologist Ferdinand von Hebra introduced resurfacing agents such as phenol and nitric acid [3]. Modern references sort peels by depth: alpha hydroxy acid peels (glycolic, lactic) as the mildest, beta hydroxy acid peels (salicylic acid) used for acne, retinoic acid peels, and deeper trichloroacetic acid and phenol-croton oil peels that must be performed by a medical provider [3].

Enzyme peels are not part of that depth classification. They are sold alongside it as a non-acid route to the same visible goal of a smoother, more even surface, aimed at people who find acid peels irritating, at first-time peel users and at those who want no downtime [3]. The same references note that stronger peels carry risks of redness, pigment change and scarring, which is the contrast brands draw when positioning enzymes as the mild option [3].

sections.h: Pharmacology and how the enzymes work
paras: Papain is a cysteine protease. Its active site uses a pair of residues, cysteine 25 and histidine 159, to attack the carbonyl carbon of a peptide bond, forming a temporary acyl-enzyme intermediate that water then releases, which splits the protein chain [1]. It prefers to cleave after arginine or lysine residues that follow a hydrophobic residue [1].

Papain is relatively heat-resistant, with an optimal range of roughly 60 to 70 degrees Celsius, and in the laboratory it is used to dissociate tissue into single cells for culture [1]. Crude papain is produced by scoring unripe papaya fruit, collecting the dried latex, and purifying it [1]. Proponents of enzyme peels describe the action on skin as a short-contact, surface-level version of this protein digestion, aimed at the keratin-rich dead cell layer; published comparisons of that action on human skin are not available [4].

Papaya enzyme masks rely on papain, which Wikipedia describes as relatively heat-resistant, with an optimum of about 60 to 70 degrees Celsius and a preference for cleaving after arginine or lysine residues [1]. Pineapple-based products rely on bromelain, a mixture of proteases [2]. Pumpkin peels are usually sold with fruit acids and are a seasonal fixture of facial menus, so a pumpkin enzyme peel may exert effects from both its enzymes and its acids [3].

Papain has also been studied outside cosmetics in immobilised form on different supports for industrial and biotechnology uses, which a 2021 review catalogues [5]. These uses show how readily the enzyme can be formulated but do not describe skin outcomes.

Papaya latex was used as a meat tenderizer in South America before European contact, and papain became the active ingredient in many commercial tenderizers [1]. Industrial uses followed in leather and textile processing, detergents and pharmaceuticals, with cosmetic uses among them [1].

Medical uses grew out of the same enzymatic action. Papain-based ointments such as Accuzyme were used to debride dead tissue from chronic wounds, and a papain gel called Papacarie is used to remove dental decay chemomechanically without drilling [1]. Bromelain-derived debridement for burns is approved in Europe as NexoBrid [2]. Enzyme masks for the face emerged in the spa and skincare market as a rinse-off counterpart sold for smoothing and brightening.

Enzyme peels are sold by spas and skincare brands in professional and at-home forms. Pumpkin enzyme peels are often paired with fruit acids and are a seasonal favourite in facial treatments, while papaya and pineapple masks draw on the commercial familiarity of papain and bromelain [1][2]. They are positioned for people who find acid peels too irritating, and for first-time peel users.

Regulatory attention has centred on papain as a drug. On 23 September 2008 the FDA warned companies to stop marketing topical papain drug products, including Accuzyme, Panafil and Ziox, by 4 November 2008, stating they had been marketed without approval [1]. These warnings concerned drug products for wound care rather than cosmetic masks.

In the laboratory comparison, pineapple flesh showed the highest specific protease activity, and two of the eleven commercial enzyme peels showed sufficient activity against casein [4]. This work measured enzyme activity in jars and tubes, not effects on human skin, and it shows that enzyme content varies between products.

Outside cosmetics, topical papain ointments have been used to clear dead or contaminated tissue from ulcers and wounds, and bromelain-based debridement is approved in Europe for burns as NexoBrid [1][2]. This debridement of dead tissue is the same enzymatic principle that cosmetic peels borrow on a much milder scale.

In September 2008 the US FDA told companies to stop marketing unapproved topical papain drug products, citing reports of serious reactions including allergic reactions with low blood pressure and rapid heart rate [1]. People with latex allergy may also react to papain because latex and papaya are related sources [1]. Cosmetic enzyme peels are a separate product category from those drug products. Bromelain supplements have no confirmed dosage or long-term safety data, according to Wikipedia's summary [2].

Latex-papaya syndrome, a cross-reaction between latex and papaya allergens, has been described in the allergy literature [6]. Wikipedia's chemical peel article notes that even mild at-home peels can irritate skin, with redness and dryness as the expected light effects [3].

Spa menus and skincare brands offer enzyme peels as a facial add-on and as a weekly at-home mask. The stated appeal is a fresher, brighter surface and smoother texture without the tingling of acids, and people with sensitive skin or those preparing for an event are among the audiences brands name. Because the 2022 laboratory work found activity varied widely between products, how a given jar behaves depends on its formulation [4].
No studies found. A 2022 laboratory study measured the enzyme activity of commercial peels but did not test skin outcomes [4].

lore.intro: Enzyme peels are described mainly in brand and spa marketing, not in forum research threads; the claims below are the ones commonly made for them.
